newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland police chief sees "dangerous situation".
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland police chief sees "dangerous situation".

text.p: Northern Ireland's police chief said on Sunday that resurgent IRA violence had created "a very dangerous situation" in the province.

Chief Constable Ronnie Flanagan, dismissing media suggestions that the Irish Republican Army was engaged in shadow boxing in the runup to British elections on May 1, said it was mounting "real attacks with a determination to kill."

He was speaking to Sky television the day after security forces found a 1,000-lb (500-kilo) bomb abandoned in a country road. Its apparent target would have been British soldiers from the nearby Ballykinler army base.
Superintendent Sam Martin said nine plastic bags of fertiliser-based explosive and detonators were being put together in an attempt to cause "appalling injury or death to passers-by."

No one claimed responsibility for the bomb, but it was thought to be the latest attempt by the IRA to attack British targets in defiance of appeals by Britain, Ireland and the United States to declare a new ceasefire.

The opposition Labour party's spokeswoman on Northern Ireland, Mo Mowlam, said a truce called now would give sufficient time for authorities to determine it was genuine and allow Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, to attend peace talks.
Her words appeared to signal no change in the policy of Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government but a Sinn Fein spokesman said they were "encourging."

Sinn Fein's ideological foes, Protestant-backed Unionist parties which want the province to stay British, say they do not believe the IRA will call a complete halt to violence unless it is guaranteed of getting a united Ireland.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), said his party would walk out if Sinn Fein were admitted to the talks.

Security sources say they believe the IRA is determined to mount what they call "spectacular" attacks before the British election to force the next government to ease conditions for Sinn Fein's entry into the negotiations.
Flanagan said he expected "difficulties" over this year's Protestant Orange Order marches after last year's parades provoked the worst civil unrest in the province for decades.
He was speaking on the eve of a Belfast march by the Apprentice Boys, a Protestant order, which heralds the official start of the so-called marching season.

Flanagan said he was not entirely pessimistic about this year's marches. "I think people witnessed the events of last summer with a certain degree of horror and I think there is a determination on the part of all right-thinking people that the events of last summer should not be repeated," he said.
But he added: "I don't want to pretend that we expect an absolutely trouble-free summer. I think I would be a fool, I would be naive to suggest that. There will undoubtedly be difficulties."
